title: Gross Anatomy of the Head and Neck (ANA 301)
description: Skull and scalp, face and cranial nerves in the face, triangles of the neck, oral cavity, pharynx and larynx, and the orbit and ear.

topics.title: Skull, Scalp and Cranial Cavity
topics.summary: Bones and foramina of the skull, layers of the scalp, dural venous sinuses and intracranial haemorrhage.

notes.b: The scalp has five layers (SCALP): Skin, dense Connective tissue (contains vessels — wounds bleed profusely), Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica), Loose areolar tissue (the 'danger area' through which infection spreads via emissary veins to the dural sinuses) and Pericranium. The pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet, overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery; fracture here causes an extradural haematoma. Key foramina: optic canal (CN II, ophthalmic artery), superior orbital fissure (CN III, IV, V1, VI), foramen rotundum (V2), foramen ovale (V3), foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery), internal acoustic meatus (VII, VIII), jugular foramen (IX, X, XI, internal jugular vein), hypoglossal canal (XII), foramen magnum (medulla, vertebral arteries).
k: SCALP layers; loose areolar = danger area
Pterion fracture → middle meningeal artery → extradural haematoma
Foramen ovale: V3; spinosum: middle meningeal artery

notes.b: The meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia mater. An extradural (epidural) haematoma is arterial (usually middle meningeal artery), biconvex/lentiform on CT, with a 'lucid interval'. A subdural haematoma results from torn bridging veins, is crescent-shaped, and is common in the elderly and alcoholics. Subarachnoid haemorrhage usually follows rupture of a berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis, presenting with sudden 'thunderclap' headache. Dural venous sinuses (superior sagittal, transverse, sigmoid, cavernous) drain into the internal jugular vein; the cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery and CN VI, with III, IV, V1 and V2 in its lateral wall.
k: CN VI runs through the cavernous sinus

topics.title: Face and Cranial Nerves V and VII
topics.summary: Muscles of facial expression, sensory supply of the face, parotid gland and facial palsy.

notes.b: The trigeminal nerve (V) gives sensation to the face via three divisions: ophthalmic (V1 — forehead, upper eyelid, cornea, nose tip), maxillary (V2 — cheek, upper lip, upper teeth) and mandibular (V3 — lower lip, chin, lower teeth, and part of the auricle), and supplies the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) via V3. The corneal reflex has its afferent limb in V1 and efferent limb in VII. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief severe stabbing facial pain. Inferior alveolar nerve block (V3) anaesthetises the lower teeth in dentistry.
k: V1, V2, V3 sensory to face
Corneal reflex: V1 afferent, VII efferent

notes.b: The facial nerve (VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression via five branches in the parotid gland (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical), taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani), and secretomotor fibres to the submandibular, sublingual and lacrimal glands. The parotid gland is traversed (superficial to deep) by the facial nerve, retromandibular vein and external carotid artery; its secretomotor supply is from the glossopharyngeal nerve (via the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve). A lower motor neuron facial palsy (e.g. Bell's palsy) paralyses the whole half of the face including the forehead; an upper motor neuron lesion (stroke) spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation.
k: Facial nerve: 5 branches in the parotid
Chorda tympani: taste anterior 2/3 of tongue
Bell's palsy (LMN) affects the forehead; stroke (UMN) spares it

topics.title: Triangles of the Neck and Thyroid
topics.summary: Anterior and posterior triangles, carotid sheath, thyroid gland and the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

notes.b: Sternocleidomastoid divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. The posterior triangle (bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and the clavicle) contains the accessory nerve (XI) — at risk in lymph node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness and inability to shrug — plus the cervical plexus branches, external jugular vein and brachial plexus trunks. The anterior triangle contains the carotid, submandibular, submental and muscular triangles. The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery (medial), internal jugular vein (lateral) and vagus nerve (posterior, between them). The common carotid bifurcates at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3/C4); the carotid sinus is a baroreceptor.
k: Posterior triangle: accessory nerve at risk
Carotid sheath: artery medial, IJV lateral, vagus posterior

notes.b: The thyroid has two lobes joined by an isthmus over the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, enclosed in pretracheal fascia, so it moves up on swallowing. It develops from the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends via the thyroglossal duct; remnants form thyroglossal cysts that move on protruding the tongue. Blood supply: superior thyroid artery (external carotid), inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk) and sometimes thyroidea ima. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove close to the inferior thyroid artery; injury in thyroidectomy causes hoarseness (bilateral injury can cause airway obstruction). The external laryngeal nerve, near the superior thyroid artery, supplies cricothyroid; injury changes voice pitch.
k: Thyroglossal cyst moves with tongue protrusion
Left RLN hooks around the aortic arch

topics.title: Oral Cavity, Pharynx and Larynx
topics.summary: Tongue, palate, tonsils, pharyngeal constrictors, larynx and its nerve supply.

notes.b: All muscles of the tongue are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII) except palatoglossus (vagus via the pharyngeal plexus). A hypoglossal lesion causes the protruded tongue to deviate towards the side of the lesion. General sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is from the lingual nerve (V3), taste via chorda tympani (VII); the posterior third receives both from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). The palatine tonsil lies in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches; peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) displaces the uvula. The pharyngeal constrictors are supplied by the vagus; the gag reflex has IX as afferent and X as efferent. Killian's dehiscence between the parts of the inferior constrictor is where a pharyngeal pouch forms.
k: Tongue deviates towards the side of a XII lesion
Gag reflex: IX afferent, X efferent

notes.b: The larynx has three unpaired cartilages (thyroid, cricoid — the only complete ring, epiglottis) and paired arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal cords. All intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve). Sensation above the vocal cords is from the internal laryngeal nerve and below from the recurrent laryngeal nerve. In airway emergencies, cricothyroidotomy is performed through the cricothyroid membrane between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

topics.title: Orbit, Eye Movements and Ear
topics.summary: Extraocular muscles and their nerves, cranial nerve palsies, and the anatomy of the ear.

notes.b: Six extraocular muscles move the eye: medial, lateral, superior and inferior recti, and superior and inferior obliques. Nerve supply: LR6 SO4 — lateral rectus by abducens (VI), superior oblique by trochlear (IV), all others (and levator palpebrae superioris) by the oculomotor nerve (III). Oculomotor palsy produces a 'down and out' eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil (loss of parasympathetic fibres — compressive lesions such as posterior communicating aneurysm affect the pupil early). Abducens palsy causes inability to abduct and horizontal diplopia; it may be an early sign of raised intracranial pressure. Horner's syndrome (sympathetic lesion) causes partial ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
k: III palsy: down and out, ptosis, dilated pupil
VI palsy: can't abduct; false localising sign

notes.b: The external ear (auricle and external acoustic meatus) is separated from the middle ear by the tympanic membrane. The middle ear contains the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), the stapedius (supplied by VII; paralysis causes hyperacusis) and tensor tympani (V3); it communicates with the nasopharynx via the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube — shorter and more horizontal in children, predisposing to otitis media — and with the mastoid air cells (mastoiditis). The inner ear contains the cochlea (hearing) and the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals for rotation; utricle and saccule for linear acceleration), innervated by the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII).
k: Short horizontal Eustachian tube in children → otitis media
